title: Closing the browser still devours hundreds of MB of memory! Chrome's hidden AI memory hog exposed — one trick shows you how to completely free up resources

content_html:
After a day of work or entertainment, you habitually click the X in the top-right corner to close Chrome, only to open Task Manager and discover that multiple Chrome processes are still stubbornly running in the background, silently eating up 300MB to 700MB of precious memory. What's even more maddening is that even if you've already turned off the "Continue running background apps after Chrome is closed" option and tried all the usual troubleshooting steps—disabling extensions, clearing the cache, resetting settings—the problem still persists.

This isn't because your computer has a virus, nor is it some rogue extension causing trouble. Recently, a developer used rigorous cross-testing (after creating a brand-new signed-out profile, the browser could exit normally) to finally track down this hidden "memory assassin"—Chrome's built-in Gemini AI feature.

The truth revealed: To stay "always ready," AI quietly took over the background

The root of the problem lies in Chrome's aggressive design for the AI experience. To enable users to "quickly summon Gemini with a keyboard shortcut even after the browser is minimized or closed," Chrome keeps the relevant background processes running at the system level.

While this design logic improves AI response speed, it comes at the cost of system resources. More insidiously, this setting's priority seems to bypass the traditional background app management options, causing many resource-conscious users to unknowingly endure unnecessary memory consumption over the long term.

The ultimate fix: Three steps to completely stop AI from staying in the background

If you want Chrome to exit completely and cleanly after you close it and release all the memory it was using, you only need to adjust one hidden setting:

1. Quick path: Enter `chrome://settings/ai/gemini` directly in Chrome's address bar and press Enter.

2. Manual path: Click the three-dot menu in the top-right corner of the browser, then go to "Settings" > "AI Innovations" > "Gemini in Chrome."

3. Key step: In the "Preferences" section, find the option "Show Gemini in Chrome in the system tray and enable keyboard shortcuts" and turn it off completely.

After doing this, close the browser again, and you'll find that the leftover processes in Task Manager have disappeared without a trace, and memory usage drops immediately.

Industry insight: AI empowerment should not come at the cost of a "resource black box"

Chrome's "memory assassin" incident reflects a common pain point across the software industry as it embraces AI: an imbalance between aggressive features and resource management.

In fact, Chromium-based browsers (including Chrome and Edge) are reserving more and more system resources for local AI models, and some data shows that their disk space usage can reach as high as 20GB. As "AI as a standard feature" becomes an industry consensus, browser makers must not turn system resource consumption into a "black box" while pursuing a "seamless, always-ready" intelligent experience.

True intelligence should not be built on plundering resources without users' knowledge. Transparent resource usage notifications and clear, easy-to-find disable options are the bottom line that software design in the AI era must uphold. While enjoying the convenience brought by AI, giving control of the system back to users is the key to winning long-term trust.
